verses.text: In the second year of Joash son of Joahaz king of Israel Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah began to reign.
He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddin of Jerusalem.
He did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes, yet not like David his father. He did according to all that Joash his father had done.
However the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.
As soon as the kingdom was established in his hand, he killed his servants who had slain the king his father,

but the children of the murderers he didn’t put to death; according to that which is written in the book of the law of Moses, as Yahweh commanded, saying, “The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children be put to death for the fathers; but every man shall die for his own sin.”
He killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, and took Sela by war, and called its name Joktheel, to this day.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash, the son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come, let us look one another in the face.”

Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as wife. Then a wild animal that was in Lebanon passed by, and trampled down the thistle.
You have indeed struck Edom, and your heart has lifted you up. Enjoy the glory of it, and stay at home; for why should you meddle to your harm, that you fall, even you, and Judah with you?’”
But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up; and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth Shemesh, which belongs to Judah.
Judah was defeated by Israel; and each man fled to his tent.

Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Jehoash the son of Ahaziah, at Beth Shemesh, and came to Jerusalem, and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits.
He took all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in Yahweh’s house and in the treasures of the king’s house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehoash which he did, and his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Jehoash slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel; and Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.
Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel fifteen years.
Now the rest of the acts of Amaziah, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
They made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish; but they sent after him to Lachish, and killed him there.
They brought him on horses, and he was buried at Jerusalem with his fathers in David’s city.
All the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the place of his father Amaziah.
He built Elath, and restored it to Judah. After that the king slept with his fathers.
In the fifteenth year of Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel began to reign in Samaria for forty-one years.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight. He didn’t depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin.

He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah, according to Yahweh, the God of Israel’s word, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath Hepher.
For Yahweh saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter; for all, slave and free, and there was no helper for Israel.
Yahweh didn’t say that he would blot out the name of Israel from under the sky; but he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.

Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, and all that he did, and his might, how he fought, and how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath, which had belonged to Judah, for Israel, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Jeroboam slept with his fathers, even with the kings of Israel; and Zechariah his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: Amaziah begins his reign in the second year of Joash of Israel—a young man stepping into a kingdom already fractured. I'm struck by how often the Lord places a new ruler amid troubled times, not to escape them but to navigate them faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-five years old, twenty-nine years to reign. He has a mother, Jehoaddin, who carries her own weight in this story. Behind many a young king is a woman who steadies his hand or lets him fall—either way, the home shapes the crown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He does right in the Lord's eyes, but 'not like David.' That honest phrase—*not like David*—reminds us that we can walk obediently and still fall short of the father of our faith. We do what we can with the heart we have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high places remain. For all his good intentions, Amaziah cannot—or will not—sweep away the old habits of the people. Sometimes our obedience is real but incomplete, and we must live with the compromises we inherit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When his grip on the kingdom is secure, he kills the men who murdered his father. Justice delayed is not justice abandoned—yet there's something unsettling in the caution that waited until his throne was firm before reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The murderers' children live. Amaziah cleaves to the Law—'each man shall die for his own sin'—though he could have erased the bloodline entirely. This verse anchors a mercy that runs deeper than vengeance: a soul answers for its own choices before the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten thousand Edomites fall in the Valley of Salt; Sela is renamed Joktheel. Military triumph can feel like blessing, and Amaziah tastes victory and names it 'God opens.'  But the heart that trusts in a great win often forgets the One who granted it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fresh from victory, Amaziah sends word to Jehoash of Israel: 'Let us look one another in the face.' A young man flushed with success reaches out to a rival. Pride whispers before the fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash answers with a parable—thistle and cedar, wild animal trampling. The image lives in memory because it cuts so cleanly: 'Your glory is small; don't reach beyond your branch lest you fall.' Wisdom speaks truth through pictures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He begs Amaziah to hear wisdom: 'Stay at home. Why meddle to your harm?' The king of Israel, himself far from perfect, pleads for his neighbor's life. Yet a heart drunk on victory hears no voice but its own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amaziah will not listen. So the two kings meet at Beth Shemesh—'House of the Sun'—not in peace but in war. Sometimes we must learn the hard way what the gentle warning tried to teach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah is defeated. Each man flees to his tent. The rout is sudden and complete—the triumph of seven verses ago crumbles in a moment. Pride's fall is often as swift as its rise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash takes Amaziah captive and breaks Jerusalem's wall from Ephraim's gate to the corner gate—four hundred cubits of stone brought low. A physical wound marks the spirit's breaking; the walls we trust in crumble when we trust in ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold, silver, vessels from Yahweh's house—all carried away to Samaria. The victor empties the sanctuary. In losing the battle, Judah loses not just dignity but the very treasures meant for worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of Jehoash's acts are written in the chronicles. Here the text pauses to mark that these things are *remembered*—recorded in the annals of Israel. Our deeds outlive us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash sleeps with his fathers, buried in Samaria among the kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam takes the throne. The line continues; power passes forward even when a king departs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amaziah lives fifteen years after Jehoash dies. A long survival through the ruins of his own folly—time to wonder, to grieve, to perhaps understand at last what pride has cost him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicles hold his deeds. But the chronicler moves swiftly past the details. Not all reigns are remembered for their strength; some are simply recorded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They conspire against him in Jerusalem and hunt him down to Lachish, then to death. Once loved, now fled and hunted—his own people turn on a broken king. The fall spreads from the battlefield to the throne room to the street.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring him home on horses to be buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in David's city. Even in death, some dignity is preserved. Even the fallen are laid with their people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azariah is sixteen when they crown him. A boy takes the throne after his father's ruin. The kingdom shifts to new hands; hope rests on a young heart. The Lord still makes kings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Azariah builds Elath and restores it to Judah—a small recovery, a reaching back toward what was lost. Youth often dreams of mending what age has broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the fifteenth year of Amaziah, Jeroboam II begins his reign—forty-one years to come. The narrative shifts kingdoms again; Israel's moment grows long while Judah grieves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He does evil in Yahweh's sight, walking in the sins of his father. Despite all the warnings in the chronicles, some men still choose the crooked path. Yet the Lord's purposes are not thwarted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam restores Israel's borders from Hamath to the Dead Sea—'according to Yahweh's word, spoken by Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, from Gath Hepher.' God's promise reaches through an evil king's hands. Prophets outlast thrones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh sees Israel's bitter affliction—slave and free alike—and there is no helper. In Israel's darkest moment, the Lord still watches. He does not turn His face when we cry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord says He will not erase Israel's name from under the sky—He *saves them by Jeroboam's hand*. Readers today hear an echo of grace in this: the Lord works through flawed men, through circumstances that look like judgment, always keeping His covenant alive. Even when we cannot see the pattern, He is at work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicles record Jeroboam's acts—his might, his battles, his recovery of Damascus and Hamath for Israel. A king's strength is written down and remembered, though his heart remains far from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam sleeps with the kings of Israel, and his son Zechariah reigns in his place. Another generation inherits the throne. The line continues; the story moves on—until it doesn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
